The same license number appeared on two rows with different statuses (Active on one, No Longer Associated on another).
Statuses seen in one result list: Active; Not Active - Expired; Not Active - Expired after a lapse; Not Active - Voluntarily Surrendered; No Longer Associated.
The summary page lists 'See also' license numbers: other licenses tied to the same business.
Result and record pages are form postbacks with no shareable URL.
recordSections: Summary: license number, status, first licensed date
Unpaid Debt (Covers past 10 years): unpaid claims, unpaid civil penalties
Administrative Suspensions (Covers past 10 years): suspended for lack of bond/insurance
Business detail: endorsement type, expiration date, entity type, workers' compensation status
Additional licenses: Certified Lead-Based Paint Renovation (LBPR) contractor license yes/no
Workers' compensation, liability insurance and surety bond (Residential and Commercial rows, each with company and amount)
Associated individuals and assumed business names

facts.claim: The license number is the most accurate search key, and contractors must print it on their advertising.
facts.quote: The most accurate way to look up a license is with a CCB license number. Contractors must put this number on their advertising, including brochures, websites, and business cards.

facts.claim: A failed name search does not mean the contractor is unlicensed; spelling and punctuation vary.
facts.quote: If you cannot find the contractor by name, do not assume they are unlicensed. When a match can't be found, it may be due to a discrepancy in the spelling or punctuation of the name.

facts.claim: Records refresh every 6 hours.
facts.quote: License records are updated every 6 hours daily

facts.claim: The record summary shows unpaid claims and penalties, complaints, discipline and bond/insurance suspensions, each covering the past 10 years.
facts.quote: Learn more about this business Unpaid Debt (Covers past 10 years) Unpaid Claims $0.00 Unpaid Civil Penalties $0.00 Complaint History (Covers past 10 years) Any complaints (claims) filed against this contractor? Disciplinary History (Covers past 10 years) Any civil penalties or other sanctions (license suspensions)? Administrative Suspensions (Covers past 10 years) Has the CCB ever suspended this contractor for lack of bond/insurance?

facts.claim: The business detail shows whether the contractor holds the lead-based paint renovation license needed for pre-1978 homes.
facts.quote: CERTIFIED LEAD-BASED PAINT RENOVATION (LBPR) CONTRACTOR LICENSE: Required to bid and work on pre-1978 residential structures.

facts.claim: The workers' compensation entry can be out of date; the CCB is not told automatically when it changes.
facts.quote: The CCB does not receive automatic notification of changes to workers’ compensation coverage status. Current Oregon coverage status can be confirmed through the Oregon Workers’ Compensation Division.

facts.claim: The record lists a Residential bond row and a Commercial bond row separately; on the record we opened, a commercial-only firm showed None for Residential.
facts.quote: SURETY BOND INFORMATION (History) Type Company Amount Residential None None None

facts.claim: The CCB license does not mean construction training, except for plumbers, electricians and a few other trades.
facts.quote: Oregon does not require contractors - other than plumbers, electricians and a few other specific trades - to have training in construction. That's why it is important to check references and research a contractor's specific skills once you verify the business is licensed.

facts.claim: To get licensed, one person completes 16 hours of training and passes an open-book exam of 80 questions with a 70 percent pass mark.
facts.quote: Complete at least 16 hours of pre-license training from an approved pre-license education provider and pass the Oregon exam. You can use the manual during the open-book exam. There are 80 multiple choice questions; a passing score is 70 percent (56 correct answers).

facts.claim: Handyman work needs a license; gutter cleaning, pressure washing for cleaning and debris clean-up do not.
facts.quote: Generally, Oregon law requires anyone who works for compensation in any construction activity involving improvements to real property to be licensed. Examples of work that does require a license include: Handyman. Examples of work that does not require a license include: Gutter cleaning Power and pressure washing for the purpose of cleaning (siding, sidewalks, etc.) Debris clean up (yard or construction site)

facts.claim: Residential General Contractor: any number of trades; $25,000 residential bond and $500,000 per occurrence insurance.
facts.quote: Residential General Contractor (RGC) These contractors may supervise, arrange for, or perform (partly or completely) an unlimited number of unrelated building trades involving any residential or small commercial structure or project. $25,000 Residential bond $500,000 per occurrence insurance

facts.claim: Residential Specialty Contractor: one or two unrelated trades, or three or more on one property if the contract is $2,500 or less; $20,000 bond, $300,000 insurance.
facts.quote: Residential Specialty Contractor (RSC) These contractors perform work involving one or two unrelated building trades for residential or small commercial projects. Alternatively, these residential contractors may perform work on a single property involving three or more unrelated building trades if the contract for labor and materials is $2,500 or less. $20,000 Residential bond $300,000 per occurrence insurance

facts.claim: Residential Limited Contractor (the handyman tier): no contract over $5,000, under $40,000 a year; $15,000 bond, $100,000 insurance.
facts.quote: Residential Limited Contractor (RLC) Expects gross sales of less than $40,000 from the construction business in the next year. Does not contract to perform work that exceeds $5,000. This is for part-time contractors who, for example, build for a hobby, for retirees, and for handyman services. $15,000 Residential bond $100,000 per occurrence insurance

facts.claim: A residential endorsement covers houses; a commercial-only endorsement does not, and working outside the endorsement is something the CCB investigates.
facts.quote: Contractors with a residential endorsement may work on residential and small commercial structures. Contractors with a commercial endorsement may work on both large and small commercial projects. Working on projects without the proper license endorsement (you’re a residential contractor working on a commercial project, for example)

facts.claim: Before filing, send the contractor a 30-day pre-complaint notice by certified mail to the address on record.
facts.quote: must give the contractor 30 days’ Pre-Complaint Notice by certified mail to the address on record with the board stating that you intend to file a complaint with the CCB.

facts.claim: On an existing house, the complaint must arrive within one year of substantial completion or the date work stopped.
facts.quote: existing structure: the complaint must be received within one year from the date the work was substantially completed or the date work ceased.

facts.claim: Most complaints carry a $50 processing fee, paid only when the CCB asks for it.
facts.quote: There is a $50 statutory processing fee for most complaints. We ask that you wait to pay this fee until payment is requested by the CCB.

facts.claim: The CCB mediates rather than decides; it reports about 70% of disputes resolve at mediation.
facts.quote: Approximately 70% of disputes are resolved in this manner. The CCB is not a decision making entity.

facts.claim: The bond pays only on a court judgment or arbitration award; small claims caps at $10,000; the bond pays no attorney fees.
facts.quote: The only path to access a contractor's bond is through a signed judgment from the court. Small Claims court has a $10,000 limit while Circuit Court does not have a limit. The residential/small commercial surety bond does not cover any attorney fees.

facts.claim: A bond payout takes at least 60 days; claims within one 90-day window can be held and paid together.
facts.quote: Bond payout will take at least 60 days from the date CCB receives a certified judgement. If multiple claims are filed within the same 90-day period, payment may be held until resolution of all claims.

facts.claim: A buyer usually can't file a CCB complaint about work the seller hired, unless the sale documents assign the claim to the new owner.
facts.quote: If you have work done before selling the property and defects are found after the sale but within one year of the end of the work, neither party may file a valid complaint unless there is an assignment in the sale agreement documents that links the new owner to the contractor

facts.claim: Hiring an unlicensed contractor loses both the bond and the CCB's mediation.
facts.quote: You lose the ability to recover damages through a bond and get CCB help mediating a dispute if you use an unlicensed contractor.

facts.claim: Agreements over $2,000 must be in writing.
facts.quote: Construction agreements for more than $2,000 must be in writing.

facts.claim: A homeowner can cancel an initial residential contract in writing before midnight of the next business day (ORS 701.310).
facts.quote: A property owner can cancel any initial contract for construction, improvement, or repair of a residential structure by giving the contractor a written notice of cancellation prior to midnight of the next business day. Some exceptions apply such as work already substantially begun. (ORS 701.310.)

facts.claim: Homebuyer Protection Act (ORS 87.007): covers new homes and existing homes with at least $50,000 of work within three months before the sale; the contractor-seller must protect the buyer from liens.
facts.quote: This law (ORS 87.007) protects home buyers from construction liens when the buyer has already paid for the construction work. An existing single-family residence, condominium unit, or residential building that had at least $50,000 worth of improvements, additions or remodeling within three months before the sale. A contractor selling a home that is subject to this law must protect the buyer from liens.

facts.claim: The contractor-seller's options include title insurance without a lien exclusion, holding 25 percent in escrow or a bond, lien waivers, or waiting out the lien deadline (usually 75 days); they complete a compliance form.
facts.quote: Buy title insurance that does not exclude filed or unfiled claims of lien Retain at least 25 percent of the sales price in escrow Maintain a bond or letter of credit for at least 25 percent of the sales price Obtain lien waivers or releases Wait to complete the sale after the deadline for filing liens (usually 75 days) Contractors must complete the form Notice of Compliance with the Homebuyers Protection Act

facts.claim: Home inspectors are certified, and must own or work for a CCB-licensed business; the CCB search page has a separate Home Inspectors search.
facts.quote: Any individual who advertises, bids, or performs residential home inspections of more than one structural component needs to be certified. Once certified, you must own or work for a business that is licensed with the Construction Contractors Board.

facts.claim: Electrical and plumbing licenses are with the Building Codes Division, linked from the CCB search page.
facts.quote: Find License Information from Other Agencies Building Codes Division — electrical and plumbing
